Trucks are taking a greater market share too, suggesting that consumer confidence may slowly be improving. - In Europe, growing concern over debt issues and the health of the Euro depressed demand for new cars as consumers delayed purchases. Demand is likely to remain weak throughout 2012 although platinum should perform better than palladium if the diesel sector stays strong as we expect. - Japanese car production continues to improve following the triple disaster of March 2011 and the disruption following the Thai floods. There are early signs of industry attempts to grow diesel car sales in this market. - Chinese car sales and production growth were disappointing last year but look likely to improve this year as the economy avoids a “hard landing”. The involvement of many branches of government in regulating this market makes forecasting tricky but we feel that the 2012 outlook is for faster growth than last year. - Brazilian and Indian sales are weaker than they were during most of 2011. Although the global automotive industry grew in Q4 2011, with both sales and producti

on 2.7 per cent above their levels in the final quarter of 2010, there was a growing sense of negativity. In Europe, the growing concern over debt issues and the health of the Euro itself depressed demand for new cars as consumers understandably delayed purchases. A sharp decline in the Rupee accompanied a rather more sedate slowdown in economic growth, weakening Indian car demand, and even the Brazilian car market slowed from its breakneck pace. Extended flooding across Thailand also hit production there and elsewhere in Asia where Thai-made components are widely used. The Chinese automotive market continued to disappoint compared to the previous year but sales and production still grew in 2011 overall compared to one year earlier. Japanese domestic vehicle production grew strongly as the recovery from march’s triple disaster progressed. Russian vehicle sales were strong too and the North American market finally flung off its lethargy, to show some reasonable growth. Overall, the gloomy feel of the market in Q4 did not seem fully justified. |**Region**|**Share**

Production| 2 **Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Pole Position** **20 February 2012** ## **Europe** General sentiment on the European economy is rather depressed. Short term issues for many of the peripheral countries in rolling over large quantities of sovereign debt are threatening the stability of the finances of a number of countries. In the short term, Greece is of greatest concern but Ireland, Italy, Portugal and Spain also face similar issues. Moves by the European Central Bank to inject capital into the banking sector has reduced the potential impact of a Greek or other default over bond payments. However, any such event would probably cut two to three per cent from Europe’s GDP this year if it occurs. Austerity measures to balance budgets in the medium term are also resultin

g in reduced public sector spending in many countries and hurting economic demand during what already appears to be another recession. Monthly EU light duty vehicle sales, million units

In this somewhat uncertain environment, companies are being careful over capital expenditure and individual consumers are behaving likewise. It is not surprising that purchasing of new cars is being delayed or cancelled by consumers. Passenger car sales in the European Union fell by 1.8 per cent year-on-year in October, 3.5 per cent in November and 6.4 per cent in December (and 1.7 per cent in 2011 overall). A further fall of 7.1 per cent in January indicates that car sales this year will be level with last year’s figure at best: it is much more likely sales will fall by a few per cent. IHS Automotive forecast a 5.9 per cent decline this year while Peugeot expects to see a 10 per cent fall in the French market. There are indications that the French Government may yet reintroduce some sales incentives to support the market so not all of the news in the European sector is bad. Manufacturing volumes will also be less affected as exports of luxury cars to China and elsewhere sustain German output in particular. **Overall, however, poor economic sentiment will equate to lower platinum group metal demand.** Looking at the individual metals, however, requires us to look at the balance between the diesel and gasoline markets. In the UK, for instance, new car registrations in January 2012 were almost level with those in January 2011. However, growth in fleet sales and a move towards fuel efficiency to offset higher fuel costs saw the market share of diesel cars rise from 50.5 per cent to 53.7 per cent of the market. New diesel model availability also boosted demand and we see this trend in market shares being repeated across Europe. **Even in a falling market, therefore, diesel car sales could rise, meaning that platinum demand should be more robust than palladium demand.** Commercial vehicle sales were healthier in 2011 than in 2010, rising by ten per cent to 1.94 million units. However, they remain more than a fifth lower than they were before the economic crisis. As might be expected, the peripheral countries which are suffering the attentions of the bond market underperformed: Italian and Spanish sales fell. However, registrations of new vans rose by 17 and 19 per cent in the UK and Germany respectively. **These vehicles are predominantly diesel-fuelled so this growth is positive for platinum demand.** The market for heavier trucks (heavy duty diesel) is healthier still: December sales climbed by 20 per cent in Spain and increased in every major national market. Vehicle purchases have been depressed for some time and some form of recovery is overdue. However, new orders will depend on

economic output and growth rates are therefore likely to moderate. 3

The underlying health of the North American economy can be gauged by looking at the heavy 40 duty diesel market. Class 8 vehicles (the largest 35 trucks) are ordered some time in advance of delivery. The backlog of orders therefore provide a 30 way to gauge underlying demand. In Canada, for instance, the backlog of Class 8 orders has reached its highest level since the start of the global economic crisis, suggesting that the economy there is quite healthy. The situation in the US is similar with new orders running ahead of 2008 and 2009 levels, **a positive for platinum demand in particular** . However, we do have some concerns over the health of the North American economy. While there has been a reasonable recovery in confidence, any further problems in Europe, a banking crisis, or an American failure to extend tax cuts later in the year could yet throw the key US economy back into recession. For the moment, though, we are cautiously optimistic. Other commentators are more positive with

some expecting light duty vehicle sales to rise from just below 13 million units last year to 14 million units. On a further positive note for platinum demand, several new diesel-fuelled light duty vehicles will be launched soon in North America. 2012 should see the launch of a diesel Cadillac ATS, a diesel Mercedes S class and a diesel Porsche Cayenne. Chrysler plans to introduce a diesel Jeep Grand Cherokee in 2013 and Audi the A6, A8 and Q5 in the same year. Although palladium continues to make some inroads into the diesel exhaust aftertreatment sector, **we expect platinum to remain the dominant metal in diesel catalysts and see this gradual expansion of the North American light duty diesel market as a positive for platinum demand** . 4
**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Pole Position** **20 February 2012** ## **Japan** Year-on-year comparisons of the Japanese automotive market will be tricky to interpret for much of 2012. The triple disaster which took place in March 2011 had, quite apart from its humanitarian impact, a strongly disruptive effect on the automotive sector with production and sales depressed in Q2 and Q3 particularly. The widespread flooding that took place in the final quarter of 2011 caused problems throughout large parts of the industry as the supply of various parts was disrupted. The industry has largely recovered from these issues and is now operating close to capacity. Assuming that no similar events occur in 2012, we would expect to see vehicle production within Japan outperforming last year’s artificially low levels. Monthly Japanese light duty vehicle

The strength of the Yen has become a major problem for the industry with the competitiveness of domestic production being adversely affected. This has resulted in the movement of some production from Japanese plants to other countries. The Government has therefore made some changes to automotive taxation rules in an effort to stimulate domestic demand and, indirectly, domestic car production. Looking forward, there are therefore reasons to be positive over the outlook for domestic sales. The Government has reduced the annual tonnage tax imposed on cars in use, making ownership a touch cheaper. It has also extended the tax breaks on the purchase of fuel efficient cars for a further three years. This should boost demand but will probably have the most positive effect on sales of smaller vehicles, with a lower beneficial impact on pgm demand than might originally have been thought. In the longer term, proposals to increase the Japanese consumption tax (similar to a sales tax or Value Added Tax) would be a negative for vehicle demand if implemented. So, for 2012 as a wh

ole, given the short term tax cuts and the recovery from last years’ disasters, the Japanese industry expects car sales to rise by nearly 20 per cent to 5 million units this year. This is in contrast to 2011 when sales of standard and small cars fell by 18.5% and mini car sales dropped by 11.4%. **With most of these cars being gasoline-fuelled, this is positive for palladium and rhodium demand.** There is also interesting news from the diesel sector. Truck sales are strong on sustained replacement demand due to new diesel emissions rules, and even rose in 2011 from 2010. Additional demand for commercial vehicles for disaster recovery initiatives and rebuilding efforts was another positive factor. There are also the first signs of a push by passenger car manufacturers to get clean diesel vehicles into the Japanese market. One example is the new Mazda CX-5 which meets Japan’s snappily-titled Post New Long Term Emissions Regulations without separate NOx aftertreatment. **Any growth in the diesel market here is positive for platinum demand.** 5
**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Pole Position** **20 February 2012** ## **China** Looking back at 2011, new vehicle sales grew by 2.45 per cent, the lowest growth rate for more than a decade. Passenger car sales were healthier, growing 5.2 per cent to 14.5 million units. The popular conception of this market is that many of these vehicles are relatively small and use only small amounts of platinum group metals in their emissions systems. This is not particularly accurate. In fact, the minivan segment grew by 12 per cent and the sports utility vehicle (SUV) segment expanded by 20 per cent last year. **Average vehicle size is therefore rising and driving palladium and rhodium demand higher. Since new emissions rules were introduced in mid-2011, loadings will be higher this year than last year (on average) and this is positive for pgm demand.** Most forecasters expect the Chinese automotive market to grow by between 8 and ten per cent this year. One worrying sign, though, is that inventory of unsold vehicles rose by 700,000 units last year. As elsewhere, rising inventories are a sign of overcapacity and demand weakness and give some cause for concern. Sales of Chinese cars outside China are starting to increase at the same time. In Peru, for instance, almost one in every six new cars sold is now Chinese-made. The low retail prices make these cars attractive to consumers in lower and middle income countries. Backing this up, China exported 815,000 vehicles last year, 50 per cent more than a year earlier. We expect to see further penetration of the major Chinese brands in South America, Eastern Europe and throughout Asia in the coming years as they look to utilise their excess production capacity. Chinese regulation of the automotive industry remains an interesting topic too. A combination of ministries and local governments are involved in some fashion. For instance, in Beijing, 400,000 new and 400,000 used cars were sold last year. Sales of new vehicles fell by fifty per cent from the previous year, following the imposition of tighter controls on car registration by the local government. **We expect to see further limits on urban car usage in coming years, a negative for pgm demand** . The recent imposition of tariffs on some US-made cars will also hurt vehicle sales to a small extent, another negative. However, comments from the central government suggest that further incentives may be put in place in the next few months to boost demand for new cars if this is required. This is one of the reasons we are bullish for pgm demand as we believe the central government sees car production within China as an important industry which must be supported appropriately. We also note that new fuel standards are being imposed in China. Low sulphur diesel will become more widely available. **The introduction of this fuel will** , on its own, help to improve urban air quality. It will also **be positive for platinum demand** as more advanced aftertreatment technology can be used and lower-polluting diesel vehicles will become more acceptable to regulators and consumers. Although 2011 disappointed many China watchers, as the graph above shows, the long term trend in this automotive market is to higher production and higher vehicle sales. 6
**Mitsui Global Precious Metals | Pole Position** **20 February 2012** Automotive analysis company, J.D.Power recently forecast that the Chinese light duty vehicle market could reach 35 million units a year by 2018, following 11 per cent growth this year. We note that this is equivalent to just under half of current global output. While we agree that the Chinese industry is set to expand further, we feel that this forecast may be a little over-ambitious. ## **Brazil** Following the Brazilian Government’s decision to increase sales tax on imported passenger cars from September, the car market has understandably slowed: foreign-made cars are more expensive and there is insufficient current manufacturing capacity to produce more vehicles domestically. In the long term, this decision, if it does not fall foul of world trade organisation rules, could lead to more companies building production facilities within Brazil. There are, though, some indications that the Go

vernment may cut these tariffs instead. 

Last year, vehicle production was some 3.4 million units, only 0.7 per cent up on a year earlier. Domestic registrations of new vehicles climbed by 3.4 per cent to 3.63 million units, with imports rising by 30 per cent. **The short term impact is negative on palladium and rhodium demand.** While eight of the first nine months of 2011 saw domestic sales outperforming the same month in 2010, the last three months all saw sales fall after this taxation decision. January 2012 sales were healthier. Roughly two thirds of new car sales in Brazil are financed and a lack of credit availability is damaging to this market. 

Of interest, although flex fuel vehicles (capable of running on gasoline or ethanol but using gasoline or three-way catalysts) still dominate this market, diesel vehicles are slowly capturing share and now represent over six per cent of new sales of light vehicles: **this is mildly positive for platinum demand** . 

## **<mark>India</mark>** 

The Indian economy slowed from its breakneck speed of expansion in the second half of 2011 and, where many commentators previously felt that a “natural” rate of growth was 8 per cent per annum, many expect slower growth this year. This has been reflected in the Indian automotive sector where the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers has commented that car sales could fall in 2012 for the first time in a decade. More positively January passenger car sales were 7.4 per cent above the level of January 2011 while production of all vehicles was 11.3 per cent higher. To give an idea of the rate of growth of this market, Maruti Suzuki became the first manufacturer to sell 10 million cars in India in early 2012. It started manufacturing in December 1983 and sold its five millionth car in early 2006. The second five million vehicles took only a further six years to produce. 

We have previously commented on the rapid increase in diesel’s market share in India. The diesel engine is taking an ever-increasing share of domestic sales, aided by government policy which subsidises diesel prices (aimed as a subsidy to the farming sector). If the Indian Government maintains this tax differential with gasoline, then the diesel engine should capture yet more of the market for new cars within India. However, there have been reports that it intends to impose additional excise duties of 80,000 Rupees on new diesel cars, something that would badly damage demand. While we cannot judge the likelihood of this tax being imposed, this does illustrate the dependence of the diesel sector (and of its platinum demand) on the actions of legislators. 

## **<mark>Rest of the World</mark>** 

Russian car sales are expected to grow by a further 12 per cent in 2012, after last year’s remarkable 40 per cent growth to 2.6 million units. Vehicle production in Thailand should return to normal late in Q1 2012 following the extensive flooding of late 2011. Most other developing markets should s

how respectable growth unless the world economy stumbles. Korean car output may struggle as European demand for cars is expected to remain weak. 7
